Extract from Smart (1989) The World's Religions, pp. 10-25, heads the dimensions: practical and ritual; experiential and emotional; narrative or mythic; doctrinal and philosophical; ethical and legal; social and institutional; material.
Smart: 'The search for an essence ends up in vagueness'; 'It is more practical to come to terms first of all not with what religion is in general but with what a religion is.'
Smart: the Passover ceremonies commemorate the Exodus from Egypt; 'As Jews share the meal, so they retrace the story. Ritual and story are bound together.'
Smart: emotions and experiences are the food on which the other dimensions feed: 'ritual without feeling is cold, doctrines without awe or compassion are dry'.

Smart: the material dimension becomes incarnate 'as buildings, works of art, and other creations', and includes natural features of special sacredness: 'the river Ganges, the Jordan, ... Mount Fuji in Japan'.
Smart: 'The point of the list is so that we can give a balanced description of the movements ... without neglecting either ideas or practices.'

Smart applies the dimensions to nationalism (national anthem, flag, memorial days, memorials to the nation's dead) but says 'it is not really appropriate to try to call them religions, or even quasi-religions'.
Smart: 'in the context of the modern study of religion there is no implication that a myth is false'; 'to the believer, very often, these narratives are history.'

Smart: a Baptist chapel in Georgia versus an Eastern Orthodox church in Romania with blazing candles and rich ikons; 'the one plain, with hymns and Bible-reading, prayers and impassioned preaching; the other ... with processions and chanting'.

Britannica: Paul's letters are the oldest New Testament material, addressing 'the immediate problems of local churches shortly after Christ's death'; the books are arranged in narrative, not chronological, order.

Britannica: Koine, Hellenistic Greek used 'from the 4th century bc until the time of the Byzantine emperor Justinian (mid-6th century ad)' in Greece, Macedonia and Greek-ruled parts of Africa and the Middle East; the language of the New Testament.
Britannica, Christianity: 'The Christian Bible consists of the Old Testament and the New Testament'; the Old Testament is the Jewish scriptures as Christians receive them.
PBS Frontline (From Jesus to Christ): 'Jesus died around 30. For 40 years, there's no written gospel of his life'; followers passed on the tradition 'orally, by telling it and retelling it'.
Britannica: 'The word gospel is derived from the Anglo-Saxon term god-spell, meaning good story, a rendering of the Latin evangelium and the Greek euangelion, meaning good news'.

PBS Frontline: 'Mark's is the first of the written gospels'; 'both Matthew and Luke used Mark, as a source'; the oral-tradition page places the first gospel about 40 years after Jesus's death around 30, after the revolt (about 70).
Britannica: 'the books of the New Testament were composed not in order to satisfy historical curiosity about the events they recount but to bear witness to a faith in the action of God'.

Christian History Institute: in his Thirty-Ninth Festal Letter of 367 the New Testament list 'is identical with the twenty-seven writings we still accept as canonical', 'regarded as the first authoritative statement on the canon'; Britannica's canon section credits Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, with delimiting the 27 books.

Christian History Institute: 'Athanasius wrote the list to end disputes about such texts as The Shepherd of Hermas or The Epistle of Barnabas, which long had been regarded as equal to the apostolic letters.'
Britannica: the Trinity is 'the unity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as three persons in one Godhead'.
Britannica: neither the word Trinity nor the explicit doctrine appears in the New Testament; the doctrine developed gradually and by the end of the 4th century had substantially the form it has kept.
Britannica: Arius taught that Christ 'was not divine but a created being'; the Council of Nicaea (325) condemned his teaching.
Britannica: the council's creed used homoousios ('of one substance') of the Son with the Father to express their absolute equality.
Britannica: the creed now called Nicene came from the Council of Constantinople in 381, 'an independent document and not an enlargement of the Creed of Nicaea'.
Britannica: a creed is 'an authoritative formulation of the beliefs of a religious community'; a brief affirmation of faith used in public worship or initiation rites.
Britannica: the Nicene Creed is 'the only ecumenical creed', accepted as authoritative by the Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Anglican and major Protestant churches.
Britannica: Western churches gradually added 'and the Son' (filioque) from the 6th century; Eastern churches have always rejected it.
Britannica: baptism is 'a sacrament of admission to Christianity', by immersion, pouring or sprinkling, with the words 'In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.'
Britannica: St. Paul taught that baptism is a 'personal sharing in the death, burial, and Resurrection of Christ'.
Britannica: infant baptism is practised by Roman Catholic, Lutheran, Anglican and Reformed churches; believer's baptism, championed by the Anabaptists, is practised by Baptists and some others.

Britannica: the Eucharist (Greek 'thanksgiving'), also Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper, commemorates the Last Supper and is 'the central act of Christian worship and is practiced by most Christian churches in some form.'
Britannica: at the Last Supper Jesus blessed bread and wine and told his disciples to 'repeat the ceremony in his memory'.
Britannica: Roman Catholic transubstantiation holds that the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood while retaining their appearance.

Britannica: Eastern Orthodoxy 'shares many beliefs with Roman Catholicism but emphasizes the invocation of the Holy Spirit'; Lutherans affirm the real presence without transubstantiation; 'Zwingli viewed the Eucharist as a symbolic memorial'; churches that see it as a memorial 'speak not of a sacrament but of an ordinance.'

Britannica: 'an annual cycle of seasons and days ... in commemoration of the life, death, and Resurrection of Jesus Christ': Christmas cycle (Advent's four Sundays, Christmas, Epiphany) and Easter cycle (Lent, Holy Week, Easter, Pentecost).
Britannica, church year: the Christmas cycle celebrates Christ's birth on December 25, a fixed date (unlike movable Easter).
Britannica: Easter 'celebrates the Resurrection of Jesus Christ on the third day after his Crucifixion.'

Britannica: early Christians kept Sunday as 'the Lord's day' for the Resurrection; the 'weekly Sunday and the annual Paschal observance of 50 days from Easter to Pentecost' formed the earliest church calendar.

Britannica: 'Lent is a 40-day period of penitential preparation for Easter ... in imitation of Jesus Christ's fasting in the wilderness'; Western churches begin on Ash Wednesday; in Eastern churches 'Lent begins on Clean Monday'.
Britannica: Lent involves 'fasting, abstinence, and almsgiving'; Christians 'often choose to give up specific pleasures, such as sweets, alcohol, or social media'.
Royal Museums Greenwich: 'Easter falls on a Sunday between 22 March and 25 April'; the first Sunday after the full Moon on or after the spring equinox; Britannica: the equinox fixed at March 21.
Britannica: Eastern Orthodox churches use the Julian calendar, so 'the Orthodox Easter celebration usually occurs later than that celebrated by Protestants and Roman Catholics.'
Britannica: Roman Catholicism has approximately 1.3 billion followers, 'the largest of the three major branches of Christianity'.

Britannica, pope: the Bishop of Rome; the church teaches he is 'the successor of St. Peter' with 'full and supreme power of jurisdiction over the universal church in matters of faith and morals'; Britannica, Roman Catholicism: Peter as the first pope.
Britannica, Roman Catholicism: the church traces its origins to Christ and the Apostles, with Peter as first pope and bishops succeeding the apostles (apostolic succession).
Britannica: a diocese is 'a territorial area administered by a bishop', divided into parishes; in Catholicism 'only the pope can divide or merge dioceses or create new ones.'

PBS NewsHour: cardinals 'under age 80' are the only electors; voting in the Sistine Chapel until a pope is chosen 'by a two-thirds majority'; ballots are burned: black smoke means no decision, 'White smoke signals that a new pope has been chosen.'
Britannica, sacrament: Roman Catholicism recognizes seven: baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist, reconciliation, anointing of the sick, marriage and holy orders.
Britannica: a sacrament is 'the visible form of an invisible grace', St. Augustine's definition.
Britannica: Protestant reformers 'generally accepted only two sacraments: baptism and the Lord's Supper'.
Britannica: Eastern Orthodox adherents live primarily in 'the Balkans, the Middle East, and former Soviet countries'.

World Council of Churches: Orthodoxy 'consists of several autocephalous (self-governing) churches: the four ancient Patriarchates of the early church, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem', the patriarchates of Russia, Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria, and churches including Greece.
Britannica: the Ecumenical Patriarch holds 'titular or honorary primacy', 'first among equals', unlike papal authority; WCC: he 'has a position as first among equals'.

Britannica: the 1054 schism was the final separation of Eastern and Western churches; causes included Rome's claims to supremacy, 'never acknowledged in the East', and the Western addition of 'and the Son' to the Nicene Creed.

WCC: 'The veneration of icons plays an important role in Orthodox worship'; Britannica: icons hold essential liturgical importance in Orthodox practice. (Icon corners in Orthodox homes are standard practice.)
Britannica: the church teaches sacred images merit veneration, while worshippers maintain a distinction between honoring icons and worshiping God alone.

WCC: 'The worship services are held in national languages, though in some churches the original liturgical languages are used rather than the vernacular'; Smart likewise names the Liturgy as central to Eastern Orthodox practice.
HISTORY: 'The new consensus is that he mailed his theses to an archbishop on October 31'; Britannica, Ninety-five Theses: he dispatched a copy to 'Tetzel's superior, Archbishop Albert of Mainz'.

TIME (2017), quoting historian Peter Marshall: 'The incident was first recorded nearly 30 years after'; 'Luther himself never mentioned it'; Marshall sees a strong case that the theses were never posted at all. The first account (Melanchthon, 1546) says Luther posted or affixed the theses on the Castle Church; it does not mention nailing.
problem: Calling Melanchthon's account the 'door-nailing story' is imprecise: his 1546 account says Luther posted (affixed) the theses on the church, and the hammer and nails are a later embellishment. A learner could take it that Melanchthon described nailing.
proposed: The story of Luther posting the theses on the church door was first recorded nearly 30 years later by Philipp Melanchthon, who does not mention nails; Luther never mentioned it, and historians debate whether they were posted at all. (Card 028.c2: 'The door-posting story was first recorded nearly 30 years later, by his colleague Philipp Melanchthon, and Luther himself never mentioned it.')

evidence: Newberry Library: 'Luther's controversial ideas were printed and reprinted within weeks of their first circulation, and copies were bought, read, and shared by eager audiences throughout Europe.'
Britannica: excommunicated January 3, 1521 after Leo X's condemnation; at Worms on April 17-18, 1521 he declined to recant unless proven wrong by 'Scripture or by reason'.

Britannica: 'salvation is a gift God alone grants to sinners who passively affirm their faith in Christ, rather than something a sinner can actively obtain through the performance of good works'; 'Scripture as the ultimate authority in matters of faith (sola scriptura)'.
Britannica: his 'translation of the Bible into German vernacular lessened the laity's dependence on what he saw as a predatory ecclesiastical authority.'
Britannica: the Reformation fractured Western Christianity into Lutheranism, Calvinism (Reformed), Anglicanism (Henry VIII's 1534 break with Rome) and Anabaptism.
Pew (2011): 'In 1910, about two-thirds of the world's Christians lived in Europe'; 'Today, only about a quarter of all Christians live in Europe (26%).'
Britannica: Pentecostalism takes its name from Pentecost, 'the Holy Spirit's descent upon the first Christians in Jerusalem' (Acts 2).

Pew: Pentecostals hold that all Christians should seek 'a post-conversion religious experience called the baptism of the Holy Spirit', with gifts including to 'prophesy', 'practice physical healing, speak in tongues'; Britannica agrees.
Pew (2011, 2010 data): 'pentecostal and charismatic Christians together make up about 27% of all Christians'.

Pew Spirit and Power: renewalists 'believe that God, acting through the Holy Spirit, continues to play a direct, active role in everyday life'; Britannica, Pentecostalism: the movement valued lay participation and empowered ordinary believers to become evangelists.
Pew (2011): 'About half are Catholic. Protestants, broadly defined, make up 37%. Orthodox Christians comprise 12% of Christians worldwide.'
Britannica: Muhammad 'born c. 570, Mecca'; 'died June 8, 632, Medina'.
BBC Religions: 'one night in 610 he was meditating in a cave on the mountain when he was visited by the angel Jibreel who ordered him to recite.'
BBC Religions: 'During the rest of his life Muhammad continued to receive these revelations. The words were remembered and recorded, and form the text of the Holy Qu'ran'.
Britannica: Khadijah, a merchant, employed Muhammad to manage a caravan and then married him, and is widely recognized as his first convert; Encyclopedia.com (UXL): her business 'took him to Syria'.
Britannica: Khadijah 'reassured him of the authenticity of his first revelations'.
Britannica: the Arabic islam literally means 'surrender'; a Muslim is one who accepts surrender to the will of God.

BBC Religions: his message 'that there is no God but Allah, and that life should be lived in complete submission to the will of Allah'; 'Muhammad's popularity was seen as threatening by the people in power in Mecca'.
BBC Religions: Muhammad took his followers from Mecca to Medina in 622, the Hijrah (migration); '622 is the year in which the Islamic calendar begins.'
Britannica: Muhammad is the last of a series of prophets including 'Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Solomon, and Jesus.'
Encyclopedia.com (Gale): 'In the Quran he is presented as a mere human person with no divine qualities'; 'In the Islamic tradition, Muhammad is a messenger of God and the seal of the prophets.'
Britannica: tawhid literally means 'making one' or 'asserting oneness'; God is 'a unity, not composed ... but simple and uncompounded'.
Britannica: the doctrine is expressed in the shahadah, 'There is no god but God and Muhammad is His prophet' (commonly rendered 'messenger').
BBC Religions: 'God has no children, no parents, and no partners'; 'Allah has no shape or form... Allah can't be seen.'
Britannica, Allah: 'there is one infraction that God will not forgive in the hereafter: the sin of associationism, or polytheism (shirk).'
Britannica: probably a contraction of al-Ilah, 'the God'; 'Allah is the standard Arabic word for God and is used by Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews as well as by Muslims.'
BBC Religions: 'Muslims have six main beliefs': Allah as the one God, angels, the holy books, the Prophets, the Day of Judgement, and Predestination.
Pew (2012): widely known articles of faith include 'God's angels exist, even if people cannot see them'.
BBC Religions: 'Allah has the knowlege of all that will happen. Muslims believe that this doesn't stop human beings making free choices.'

Pew: 'affirmation that there is one God and Muhammad is His Prophet is nearly unanimous in most of the 39 countries'; belief in fate 'ranges from fewer than half in Albania to over nine-in-ten in Azerbaijan and Turkey' (44%, 93%, 92%).
BBC Religions: Shahadah (profession of faith), Salat (prayers five times each day), Zakat (alms for the poor), Sawm (fasting during Ramadan), Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca).

BBC: the pillars provide 'the framework of a Muslim's life, and weaves their everyday activities and their beliefs into a single cloth of religious devotion'; 'Islam regards it as pointless to live life without putting that faith into action'.

BBC: reciting the shahadah (in front of witnesses) 'is all that anyone need do to become a Muslim', said 'with total sincerity'; Encyclopedia.com calls its recitation the only requirement for conversion.
BBC: zakat is 'the systematic giving of 2.5% of one's wealth each year to benefit the poor'; Britannica: 'one-fortieth of cash and savings beyond a minimal threshold (nisab)'.
BBC: zakat 'is regarded as a type of worship and of self-purification' and helps a person acknowledge 'that everything comes from God on loan'.
Britannica: every adult Muslim must make the hajj 'at least once in his or her lifetime' if physically and financially able.
Britannica, salat: fajr (dawn), zuhr (midday), asr (afternoon), maghrib (sunset), isha (evening).
Britannica: 'The muezzin (one who gives the call for prayer) chants aloud from a raised place (such as a tower) in the mosque.'
BBC: Muslims must be clean before they pray, by ritual washing called wudhu; 'Mosques have washing facilities.' Britannica: ablutions involve 'washing of hands, face, and feet'.
Britannica: 'The Kaaba ... is a cube-shaped shrine near the center of the Great Mosque'; it is the direction (qiblah) Muslims face in their daily prayers.
Britannica: 'the mihrab, a semicircular niche reserved for the imam to lead the prayer, points to the qiblah, i.e., the direction of Mecca.'
Britannica: each rak'ah includes standing (with Quran recitation), genuflection and two prostrations; 'God is great' is recited with each change in posture.
BBC: 'each individual Muslim is in direct contact with Allah. There is no need of a priest as an intermediary. (While there is a prayer leader in the mosque, the imam, they are not a priest'.
BBC: 'Muslims can pray anywhere, but it is especially good to pray with others in a mosque'; praying together shows 'all are equal in the sight of Allah.'
Britannica: on Fridays the midday prayer is replaced by the congregational Jumu'ah, which 'includes two sermons (khutbah) delivered from the pulpit.'

Britannica: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar; Muslims fast 'from dawn until dusk'. BBC Religions (Sawm): during daylight adult Muslims give up food or drink, smoking and sexual activity.
Britannica: 'pregnant or nursing women, children, the old, the ill, the disabled, travelers on long journeys' are exempt.
Britannica: a predawn meal, suhur, and the iftar after sunset, which traditionally begins with dates, following Muhammad's custom.
Britannica: 'fasting is prescribed for you ... so perhaps you will become mindful of God'; BBC (Sawm): reasons include 'Learning self-discipline' and 'Sharing the sufferings of the poor'.

Britannica, Ramadan: the fast also demands avoiding immoral behavior, false words or bad deeds being deemed as destructive of a fast as eating; BBC (Sawm): Muslims 'are also expected to do their best to avoid evil thoughts and deeds'.
Britannica: the revelation of the Quran began in one of Ramadan's last ten nights (in 610), commemorated as Laylat al-Qadr, the 'Night of Power'.
Britannica: Ramadan ends with Eid al-Fitr, 'the Feast of Fast-Breaking', one of Islam's two major holidays, with new clothes, gifts, family meals and prayers.
BBC: Muslims are 'thanking Allah for the help and strength that he gave them throughout the previous month to help them practise self-control.'
Britannica: Eid al-Adha 'begins on the 10th of Dhu al-Hijjah', marking the culmination of the hajj, and commemorates Abraham's readiness to sacrifice his son Ishmael, spared when a ram was provided.
Britannica: after communal prayers families 'sacrifice an animal', dividing the meat: 'one for the poor, one for relatives and friends, and one for the family's household.'
Britannica: the pilgrimage runs 'from the 7th to the 12th day of Dhu al-Hijjah', the last month of the Islamic year.
Britannica: pilgrims are 'required to walk around the Kaaba counterclockwise seven times.'

BBC Religions: Hajira (Hagar) 'ran up and down two hills called Safa and Marwa' seeking help for Is'mail, until a spring gushed forth (Zam Zam); Britannica, hajj: pilgrims run between Safa and Marwah seven times.

BBC: pilgrims 'travel to the valley of Arafat and stand in the open praising Allah', spend the night at Muzdalifa, then at Mina 'throw the stones at pillars called Jamraat. These represent the devil.'
Britannica: pilgrims offer 'an animal in commemoration of Abraham's sacrifice'; 'Male pilgrims' heads are then usually shaved, and female pilgrims remove a lock of hair'.
Britannica: pilgrims enter ihram, 'the state of holiness and purity'; men wear 'two white seamless sheets' while women may wear sewn garments.
BBC: the hajj shows 'that everyone is equal in the eyes of Allah', 'stripping away all markers of social status, wealth, and pride'; pilgrims wear simple white clothes called Ihram.
